title: Automated decisions: Notice and recourse remain distinct rights
desc: Compares changing Colorado frameworks combining provider duties, consumer rights and enforcement, requiring careful version and status checks.

kps.k: The cluster frames automated-decision accountability as a combination of provider duties, consumer rights and public enforcement.
kps.d: The Colorado frameworks and the New York proposal described in the April 2024 NYSBA report address discrimination, transparency and human oversight rather than AI productivity. Their coverage differs: Colorado S.B. 26-189 reaches technology that materially influences consequential decisions, including decision assistance, across employment, housing, lending and other specified domains. The New York proposal’s quoted legislative intent focuses on decisions without human intervention. These are legislative provisions and proposals, not empirical evidence that safeguards reduce harm; the material contains no direct adversarial debate.

qs.q: May 6, 2026 ^L            The bill defines an "automated decision-making technology"     (ADMT) as a technology that processes personal data and uses     computation to generate output, including predictions, recommendations,     classifications, rankings, scores, or other information that is used to make,     guide, or assist a decision, judgment, or determination concerning an     individual.
qs.a: Colorado Senate Bill 26-189: Automated Decision-Making Technology · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The section on legislative intent says, in part:      [T]he legislature declares that any New York resident affected by any system     making decisions without human intervention be entitled to certain rights and     protections to ensure that the system impacting their lives do so lawfully, properly,     and with meaningful oversight.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations of the New York State Bar Association Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The Colorado materials describe a change in regulatory design, not a single cumulative compliance regime.
kps.d: The superseded 2024 enactment imposed reasonable-care duties for high-risk AI and linked rebuttable compliance presumptions to documentation, risk management, impact assessments, annual reviews and reporting. Its affirmative defense separately required a recognized risk-management framework and measures to discover and correct violations. The S.B. 26-189 summary describes replacement requirements centered on developer documentation, material-update notices and at least three years of compliance records. The New York proposal adds pre-deployment testing, mitigation and continuing monitoring, and defines discrimination to include unjustified differential treatment or impact. These differences concern legal design; they do not establish which approach works better.

qs.q: The bill repeals and reenacts those provisions with new           requirements regarding the use of automated decision-making technology                                 SENATE           in consequential decisions.
qs.a: Colorado Senate Bill 26-189: Automated Decision-Making Technology · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Automated systems shall undergo pre-deployment testing, risk identification and mitigation, and shall also be subjected to ongoing monitoring that demonstrates they are safe and effective based on their intended use, mitigation of unsafe outcomes
qs.a: Report and Recommendations of the New York State Bar Association Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Notice and meaningful recourse recur across the frameworks, but human reconsideration and an alternative to automation are distinct rights.
kps.d: The 2024 Colorado framework offered data correction and appeal, with human review where technically feasible. The S.B. 26-189 summary specifies interaction-stage notice, a plain-language account of the system’s role within 30 days of an adverse consequential decision, data correction and meaningful human reconsideration. The New York proposal also lists opting out and working with a human instead of an automated system. Operationally, these provisions call for more than a generic AI disclosure: organizations would need information-request, correction and review processes. Colorado’s amended excerpt qualifies some system-information disclosures by what developers supply and delegates disclosure details to sector-sensitive rulemaking.

qs.q: A deployer is required to provide     a consumer with a plain language description of a covered ADMT's role     within 30 days after the covered ADMT makes a consequential decision     that results in an adverse outcome for the consumer.
qs.a: Colorado Senate Bill 26-189: Automated Decision-Making Technology · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The bill     also grants consumers the right to request meaningful human review and     reconsideration following a covered ADMT making a consequential     decision resulting in an adverse outcome.
qs.a: Colorado Senate Bill 26-189: Automated Decision-Making Technology · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Colorado couples public enforcement with compliance accommodations while limiting some contractual transfers of discrimination liability.
kps.d: The 2024 enactment gave the attorney general exclusive enforcement authority. The S.B. 26-189 summary retains attorney-general enforcement through consumer-protection law, specifies a 60-day notice and cure opportunity where cure is possible, and creates no new private right of action. It instead allocates fault in existing discrimination actions. Both Colorado frameworks recognize qualifying sector-specific legal oversight. The replacement text also voids certain developer–deployer indemnity provisions covering a party’s own discriminatory acts or omissions, making contract allocation a practical compliance issue. An incompletely supplied developer exception prevents treating that restriction as absolute.

qs.q: The act grants the attorney general rule-making authority to implement, and exclusive authority to enforce, the requirements of the act.
qs.a: SUPERSEDED — Colorado S.B. 24-205: 2024 Automated-Decision-System Enactment · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Before initiating an action, the     attorney general must provide the developer or deployer with a 60-day     notice and opportunity to cure the alleged violation, if a cure is deemed     possible.
qs.a: Colorado Senate Bill 26-189: Automated Decision-Making Technology · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Version and status checks must precede reliance on the provisions or implementation dates.
kps.d: The supplied 2024 Colorado source is marked superseded; its original February 2026 duty start date does not establish current obligations. S.B. 26-189 combines an introduced-bill summary with amended excerpts and conflicting signed-act and second-reading labels. Its text specifies January 1, 2027 effectiveness subject to an unprovided exception. The NYSBA excerpt describes proposed New York legislation and establishes neither enactment nor task-force endorsement. Practitioners therefore need the operative text, applicable exceptions and implementing rules before fixing compliance deadlines or advising on required safeguards.

qs.q: Bill Summary:  On and after February 1, 2026, the act requires a developer of a high-risk artificial intelligence system (high-risk system) to use reasonable care to protect consumers from any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination in the high-risk system.
qs.a: SUPERSEDED — Colorado S.B. 24-205: 2024 Automated-Decision-System Enactment · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The selected regulators, courts and professional-body materials support the proposition that automated-decision accountability combines provider obligations, distinct consumer rights and public enforcement—and, in particular, that notice is not a substitute for recourse. Across the sources, disclosure is treated separately from correction, appeal, meaningful human reconsideration, opt-out or access to a human alternative. They also support the need for careful version and status checks: the Colorado materials describe changing rather than cumulative frameworks, while the New York material reports proposed legislation rather than established law or demonstrated effectiveness. Material internal variation concerns scope and regulatory design, not the core proposition. Colorado S.B. 26-189 covers systems materially influencing consequential decisions and provides post-adverse-decision human reconsideration; the superseded 2024 Colorado framework conditioned human review on technical feasibility and relied on reasonable-care presumptions; the New York proposal addresses decisions without human intervention and separately lists opt-out and human-alternative rights. Enforcement and compliance accommodations also differ. Because these are legislative provisions and proposals, they establish regulatory approaches but do not provide empirical evidence that the safeguards prevent harm. The sources are curated examples and should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: The bill     also grants consumers the right to request meaningful human review and     reconsideration following a covered ADMT making a consequential     decision resulting in an adverse outcome.
qs.a: Colorado Senate Bill 26-189: Automated Decision-Making Technology · Regulators & courts · 2026

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that automated-decision accountability combines provider duties, distinct consumer rights and public enforcement. Both describe safeguards against algorithmic discrimination and mechanisms for human oversight, but they contribute different parts of the framework. The New York material articulates a broad rights catalogue in which notice, explanation, opt-out and the ability to work with a human are separate protections; it also proposes pre-deployment testing and ongoing monitoring. The superseded Colorado enactment more explicitly joins deployer governance measures—risk-management programs, impact assessments and annual reviews—to notice, data correction and appeal through human review, backed by exclusive attorney-general enforcement. Material variation remains: New York concerns proposed legislation focused on decisions without human intervention, whereas Colorado documents an enacted but now-superseded high-risk-AI framework and makes human review conditional on technical feasibility. Neither source provides empirical evidence that these safeguards reduce harm, and the Colorado source’s superseded status reinforces the proposition’s warning that version and legal-status checks must precede reliance.

The sole curated 2026 source supports the proposition that automated-decision accountability combines provider duties, consumer rights and public enforcement, and particularly that notice and recourse are distinct safeguards. Colorado S.B. 26-189 separately provides interaction-stage notice, a post-adverse-outcome explanation, correction rights, and meaningful human review and reconsideration. It also assigns documentation and record-retention duties to developers and deployers and relies principally on attorney-general enforcement. Material internal qualifications concern implementation rather than the proposition’s core: disclosure content may vary by sector and require rulemaking; some information depends on what developers supply; the bill creates no new private right of action; and conflicting version labels mean the operative text and effective date must be verified before reliance. Because this period contains only one curated source, its position should not be generalized to all 2026 legislators or regulatory approaches.
